hint: Every group has four hex digits.

prompt: In the address 2001:db8::1, how many groups of zeros does the :: stand for?
hint: Count the groups that are written, then subtract from eight.

prompt: Three of these are correct ways to write 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001. Which one is not?
hint: How many times may :: appear?

choices.why: Valid: :: replaces the first run of two zero groups.
Valid: :: replaces the second run instead. RFC 5952 prefers the first, but both mean the same address.
Right. Two :: are ambiguous: nobody knows how many zeros each hides.
Valid: leading zeros may stay, and zero groups may be written as 0.

prompt: A colleague searches a log for 2001:0db8:0020:0010 and finds nothing, though srv appears in it many times. Why?
hint: How does Linux print srv's address?

choices.text: The log stores addresses in binary
choices.why: Logs are text; the problem is which text.

choices.text: Programs write it in the short form, 2001:db8:20:10::10
choices.why: Right. srv is logged as 2001:db8:20:10::10: same 128 bits, different text.

choices.text: The prefix changed when srv rebooted
choices.why: srv's address was given by hand and does not change.

choices.text: Leading zeros make it a different address
choices.why: They do not: dropping leading zeros keeps the value.

prompt: In 2001:db8:20:10::10/64, the first 64 bits name the network and the last 64 bits are the interface ___
hint: The figure labels the right-hand half.

prompt: A PC's MAC address is 02:5a:11:3c:d4:e7. By modified EUI-64, its link-local address is fe80::___
hint: Split, insert ff:fe, flip the bit, drop leading zeros.

prompt: Put the steps of building pc1's link-local address from its MAC in order.
hint: The figure in this section.
items: Flip the seventh bit of the first byte
trap: Flipping the bit last of all is harmless only by luck: the bit belongs to the first byte, which moves nowhere, but writing the address before flipping gives 02 where 00 belongs.

prompt: ping -c 1 fe80::1f:23ff:fee7:e9d5 printed a warning and lost its packet; with %eth0 added, r1 answered. Why was %eth0 needed?
hint: How many interfaces have a fe80::/64?

choices.text: fe80::/64 is on every link, so it names none
choices.why: Right. %eth0 is the zone: which link to send it on.

choices.text: r1 ignores pings that do not name its interface
choices.why: r1 never sees the name; %eth0 is read by pc1 alone.

choices.text: It switches ping from IPv4 to IPv6
choices.why: Both pings were IPv6; the address says so.

choices.text: It tells ping which MAC address to use
choices.why: The MAC is found by Neighbour Discovery, not by the zone.

prompt: A server's log shows a client whose interface identifier is 021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e. What can you say about the client's network card?
hint: Undo the three steps.

choices.text: Its MAC is 02:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e
choices.why: That forgets to flip the bit back: 02 becomes 00.

choices.text: Its MAC is 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e
choices.why: Right. Drop ff:fe, flip the seventh bit back: 02 becomes 00, a manufacturer's MAC.

choices.text: Its MAC is 1a:2b:ff:fe:3c:4d
choices.why: ff:fe was inserted by EUI-64 and is not part of the MAC.

choices.text: Nothing: the identifier is random
choices.why: The ff:fe in the middle is the mark of an identifier built from a MAC.

prompt: Where does an fe80:: address on a Linux PC come from?
hint: No server is involved.

choices.text: A DHCPv6 server hands it out
choices.why: Link-local addresses need no server.

choices.text: The router gives it in its advertisement
choices.why: The advertisement carries a global prefix; fe80:: is built before any router speaks.

choices.text: The interface builds it for itself when it comes up
choices.why: Right. Every IPv6 interface has one, with no configuration.

choices.text: An administrator types it into the network settings
choices.why: It is built automatically; nobody typed pc1's.

prompt: r1's advertisement gave the prefix a valid time of 86400 seconds. How many hours is that?
hint: 3600 seconds to the hour.

prompt: pc2's default route is via fe80::1f:23ff:fee7:e9d5 dev eth0. Whose address is that?
hint: Look at the last line of rdisc6.

choices.text: The switch's
choices.why: sw1's bridge address is fe80::6a:dcff:fe93:3b8a.

choices.text: pc2's own link-local address
choices.why: pc2's is fe80::fd:f2ff:fed2:63ba.

choices.text: r1's link-local address
choices.why: Right. The advertisement came from it, and IPv6 gateways are link-local.

choices.text: The provider's router, isp
choices.why: isp is on the other side of r1, on another link.

prompt: radvd on r1 stops and sends no more advertisements. What happens on pc2?
hint: Three lifetimes were advertised: 300, 14400 and 86400 seconds.

choices.text: Its global address disappears from eth0 at once
choices.why: Nothing removes it until its lifetimes run out.

choices.text: pc2 falls back to asking a DHCPv6 server for a new address
choices.why: The advertisement said there is no stateful configuration here.

choices.text: The route goes first, the address later
choices.why: Right. Router lifetime 300 s, preferred 4 hours, valid 24 hours.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because SLAAC addresses are permanent
choices.why: Both the address and the route carry lifetimes that count down.

prompt: The prefix line Autonomous address conf.: Yes tells each machine on the link to ___ its own address from the prefix.
hint: SLAAC: nobody hands it out.

prompt: Which of these did pc2 learn from r1's advertisement? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the rdisc6 output line by line.

choices.why: The Prefix line.

choices.text: That r1 is a default router for 300 seconds
choices.why: Router lifetime: 300.

choices.text: The address 2001:db8:20:10:fd:f2ff:fed2:63ba
choices.why: pc2 built that itself from the prefix and its MAC.

choices.text: That no DHCPv6 server hands out addresses
choices.why: Stateful address conf.: No.

choices.text: The address of a DNS server
choices.why: rdisc6 printed no DNS server in this advertisement.

prompt: The solicited-node multicast address for 2001:db8:20:10::1 is ff02::1:___
hint: ff followed by the last 24 bits.

prompt: ping -w 2 ff02::1%eth0 sent 2 requests and reported 2 received, +8 duplicates. How many interfaces answered each request?
hint: Ten replies in all.

prompt: One of the answers to pc1's ping to ff02::1 came from fe80::25:70ff:febc:29c6, in 0.716 ms. Who was that?
hint: Compare it with pc1's MAC, 02:25:70:bc:29:c6.

choices.text: r1, the router
choices.why: r1 is fe80::1f:23ff:fee7:e9d5.

choices.text: pc1 itself
choices.why: Right. pc1 is a member of all-nodes too, and its reply never left the machine.

choices.text: The switch sw1
choices.why: The bridge answered from fe80::6a:dcff:fe93:3b8a.

choices.text: srv, the server
choices.why: srv is fe80::9e:43ff:fe3e:caae.

prompt: Match each address to what it reaches on this office's link.
hint: Groups start with ff02.

pairs.right: Whoever has an address ending in 00:00:10

prompt: getent ahosts web listed 2001:db8:99::80 before 192.0.2.80. What does a program that tries the addresses in order do first?
hint: The list is the order.

choices.text: Connects to 192.0.2.80, since IPv4 is older
choices.why: The order is the system's preference, and here IPv6 is first.
Right. IPv6 first, IPv4 if that fails.

choices.text: Opens both and uses whichever is faster, every time
choices.why: That is what browsers do (Happy Eyeballs); a plain program goes in order.

choices.text: Asks the router which protocol to use
choices.why: The router is not asked; the choice is made on pc1.

prompt: A user says a site hangs from their PC. curl -4 to the site works at once; curl -6 hangs. Where do you look next?
hint: Two stacks, two paths.

choices.text: At the site's web server
choices.why: It answered over IPv4 at once, so it is up.

choices.text: At the PC's DNS resolver
choices.why: The name resolved for both; curl got as far as connecting.

choices.text: At the IPv6 path: routes, gateway, firewall
choices.why: Right. IPv4 working says nothing about IPv6.

choices.text: At the PC's network card, its cable and the switch port
choices.why: The card carried the IPv4 request fine.

prompt: In DNS, a name's IPv4 address is in its A record and its IPv6 address is in its ___ record.
hint: Four times the letter.

prompt: In this lab, r1's only nftables rules are an IPv4 NAT table, of family ip. What happens to IPv6 traffic through r1?
hint: A table of family ip sees IPv4 alone.

choices.text: It is translated to 203.0.113.2 as well
choices.why: NAT rules in an ip table touch IPv4 packets alone.

choices.text: It is dropped until somebody writes IPv6 rules
choices.why: There is no rule to drop it; the curl -6 tests worked.

choices.text: It is filtered by the same rules
choices.why: The rules are of family ip; IPv6 is a different family.

choices.text: It is forwarded unfiltered, both ways
choices.why: Right. Fine in a lab, and a hole anywhere else.

prompt: In the web server's capture, which source address did pc1's IPv4 connection arrive from?
hint: What does r1 do on the way out?

choices.why: pc1's address was rewritten by r1's NAT.
That is r1's inside address.
That is the web server's own address.
Right. r1's outside address, the source of everything the office sends out.

prompt: The IPv4 handshake offered mss 1460 and the IPv6 one mss 1440, on the same 1500-byte links. How many bytes longer is the IPv6 header?
hint: The TCP header is the same in both.

prompt: An office turns on IPv6: every PC gets a global address by SLAAC, and nobody writes IPv6 firewall rules. What has changed for the PCs?
hint: What did NAT do as a side effect?

choices.text: Outside machines are able to start connections to them
choices.why: Right. NAT hid them by accident; now the firewall has to decide.

choices.text: Nothing, since SLAAC addresses are private
choices.why: Global addresses from SLAAC are routed on the internet.

choices.text: Their IPv4 traffic now leaves without NAT
choices.why: IPv4 still goes through r1's NAT; the two stacks are separate.

choices.text: They lose their IPv4 addresses
choices.why: Dual stack keeps both.

prompt: IANA handed its last IPv4 blocks to the regional registries on 3 February ___
hint: APNIC ran out two months later.

prompt: Written out in full, with no group shortened, how many hexadecimal digits does an IPv6 address have?
hint: Eight groups.

prompt: pc2 has just come up with only its link-local address, and it is about to ping srv by its global address. Put what happens in order.
hint: Address first, then the neighbour, then the ping.
items: pc2 sends a Router Solicitation to ff02::2
r1 answers with a Router Advertisement
pc2 builds a global address from the prefix
pc2 asks ff02::1:ff00:10 who has srv's address
pc2 sends the echo request to srv's MAC
trap: The neighbour solicitation cannot come first: pc2 has no global address to ask from until the advertisement arrives.

prompt: Which of these IPv6 addresses is link-local?
hint: Link-local starts with fe80.

choices.why: A global address, pc2's.
A multicast group, all nodes.
The loopback address.

choices.text: fe80::9e:43ff:fe3e:caae
choices.why: Right. srv's link-local address.
